book.title: Cardiac Rehabilitation (Coronary Artery Disease, Post-MI, PCI and CABG)
book.lead: Exercise is medicine for the heart, but it must be prescribed with precision.

blocks.text: Coronary artery disease (CAD) narrows the arteries supplying the heart muscle. A partial or temporary mismatch causes **angina**; a blocked artery causes **myocardial infarction (MI)**. Treatment may include medication, **percutaneous** **coronary intervention (PCI, stent through an artery in the wrist or groin)**, or **coronary artery bypass grafting** **(CABG, open-heart surgery through the sternum)**.

Cardiac rehabilitation is a structured program of exercise, education, risk factor management and psychological support. It reduces cardiovascular mortality and hospital readmissions and improves quality of life [Ref – to verify Cochrane review].

rows: Supervised program, typically starting within weeks of discharge

sections.title: B. Recognize the presentation and risk factors

blocks.text: Modifiable risk factors: smoking, hypertension, raised cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, stress. Non-modifiable: age, male sex, family history.

rows: Event, date, treatment (PCI, CABG), complications, ejection fraction?
Any chest pain since? When, how relieved (GTN)?
Activity before the event and goals?
Mood, anxiety, return to work, driving, sexual activity concerns?

blocks.text: Resting HR, BP, SpO2, rhythm if monitored; wound check (sternum, leg graft site after CABG; groin or wrist after PCI); sternal stability; functional capacity (6MWT, shuttle walk test, or exercise test results); body mass index and waist circumference.

sections.title: E. Risk stratification and exercise testing

blocks.text: Patients are commonly classed as low, moderate or high risk using exercise capacity, ejection fraction, ischaemia or arrhythmia on testing, and complications [Ref – to verify AACVPR criteria]. Higher-risk patients need closer supervision and ECG monitoring.

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Chest pain at rest or not relieved by rest and GTN within minutes
Stop; call emergency services; follow GTN and aspirin protocol as prescribed
New palpitations with dizziness or collapse
Stop; emergency response; begin CPR and use AED if unresponsive without normal breathing
Sternal clicking, wound discharge, fever after CABG
Groin swelling or pain after femoral PCI

blocks.label: STOP AND THINK
body: Every cardiac rehabilitation session must have emergency procedures, a defibrillator, and staff trained in basic or advanced life support.

steps: **Phase I:** progressive mobilisation from sitting to walking and stairs before discharge.
**Phase II:** supervised aerobic and resistance training with monitoring.

blocks.text: Traditional precautions restrict lifting and pushing for about 6 to 8 weeks. Many centres now use more individual, movement-based approaches ("Keep Your Move in the Tube": keep upper arm movements close to the body during loaded tasks) [Ref – to verify]. Follow the surgical team's protocol.

rows: 10 to 15 min of gradually increasing low-intensity activity (important to prevent ischaemia)
20 to 40 min; 3 to 5 days a week; intensity 40 to 70% HRR or RPE 11 to 14; keep HR at least about 10 beats below any ischaemic threshold [Ref – to verify]
Start after the early phase as cleared (later for sternotomy); 1 to 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps at RPE 11 to 13, major muscle groups, 2 to 3 days a week; avoid breath holding
Risk factors, medication, recognising symptoms, GTN use, diet, smoking, stress, return to work and driving

blocks.text: Use RPE when on beta-blockers. Circuit and interval formats are acceptable for suitable patients.
Not applicable. Home monitoring devices (pedometers, heart rate monitors) support adherence.
Phase I to III as above. Long-term goal: at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week plus strength training [Ref – to verify].
Functional capacity (6MWT, METs), risk factor profile, quality of life, anxiety and depression scores, return to valued activities.

blocks.label: CLINICAL CASE
body: A 58-year-old man, 3 weeks after inferior MI treated with a stent. Ejection fraction preserved. On a beta-blocker. Resting HR 62, BP 126/78. No angina since. Goal: return to work as a schoolteacher.

items: **How will you set intensity?** RPE 11 to 14, because the beta-blocker blunts HR response.
**Why a longer warm-up?** It reduces the risk of ischaemia and arrhythmia.
**He develops chest tightness during cycling that eases with rest in 2 minutes. Action?** Stop, monitor, document; inform the medical team; set the next intensity below this threshold.
**What risk factors will you address?** Smoking, BP, cholesterol, diabetes, weight, inactivity, stress.
**Why does cardiac rehabilitation matter?** It reduces mortality and readmission and improves quality of life.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Describe the phases of cardiac rehabilitation.
Prescribe safe aerobic and resistance exercise.
Apply sternal precautions and emergency procedures.
